teenKit.tldr: The legendary 19th-century panic over absinthe's "Green Fairy" was completely overblown by terrible science, as modern forensic testing of actual vintage bottles proved its toxic chemical levels were totally safe.
teenKit.whyItMatters: It proves how easy it is for society to create a mass moral panic and blame a mysterious scapegoat while completely ignoring the real, underlying culprit—in this case, massive alcohol poisoning.
keyTakeaways: A 19th-century French scientist named Valentin Magnan created the absinthe myth by injecting animals with massive, lethal doses of pure wormwood oil instead of testing actual drinks.
Modern gas chromatography (GC-MS) testing of sealed, pre-1915 Pernod Fils bottles proved their thujone levels were well below modern legal safety limits.
The real nightmare of "absinthism" wasn't magical fairy hallucinations, but the severe reality of 70% ABV alcohol abuse and poisoning.

vocab.meaning: A chemical compound found in wormwood that historical panic blamed for causing seizures and hallucinations in absinthe drinkers.
A widespread, exaggerated fear that a certain group or habit is threatening the moral fabric of society.

quiz.question: How did the original anti-absinthe scientist Valentin Magnan test the safety of the drink in the 1800s?
options: He gave standard glasses of diluted absinthe to human volunteers in a controlled clinical trial.
He injected dogs and guinea pigs with lethal, concentrated streams of pure wormwood oil.
He used gas chromatography machines to scan sealed antique bottles from Paris cafes.
He interviewed chronic absinthe drinkers about their daily habits and psychological states.
quiz.explanation: Magnan used extreme, unrealistic animal testing by pumping massive, pure doses of wormwood oil directly into animals to manufacture terrifying results.

quiz.question: What did modern forensic scientists find when they tested actual sealed pre-1915 bottles of Pernod Fils absinthe?
options: The thujone levels were dangerously high and well above any legal threshold.
The bottles had completely evaporated into harmless dust over the course of a century.
The thujone levels averaged 25.4 mg/L, which safely sits below the modern EU legal limit.
The liquid had chemically transformed into a powerful synthetic hallucinogen.
quiz.explanation: Lachenmeier's audit shattered the myth by showing that vintage absinthe contained very modest amounts of thujone that easily cleared safety regulations.

quiz.question: If thujone wasn't turning Belle Époque artists into raving lunatics, what was the actual primary culprit behind "absinthism"?
options: Massive, chronic poisoning from drinking extremely high-proof (70% ABV) alcohol.
A lethal bacterial infection spreading through unwashed Parisian sugar cubes.
Poisonous heavy metals leaching out of the slotted silver spoons.
A completely unrelated strain of seasonal influenza unique to 1890s France.
quiz.explanation: The horrifying symptoms of absinthism were ultimately driven by the sheer destructive force of heavy, daily abuse of 70% alcohol.
